More than 2,200 universities in over 130 countries run the Hult Prize, and the field includes Harvard, Stanford and McGill. Here is how the competition works, and how Windsor fits into it.
aboutCompetition: The Hult Prize is an annual worldwide student competition. Teams of two to four build a for-profit social enterprise that addresses a United Nations Sustainable Development Goal, and pitch it in four minutes. It is often called the Nobel Prize for students, and it draws something like 250,000 student entrepreneurs a year from more than 2,200 universities across over 130 countries.

It runs in stages. Campus rounds like ours come first. The winner advances to the National Championships, and from there teams move toward the global final, where one of them receives $1 million USD in seed funding.

The for-profit part is deliberate, and it is the hardest part of the competition. A business that pays for itself keeps solving the problem after the grant money runs out, so teams are asked to build something that stands on its own rather than something that needs funding forever.
aboutWindsor: We run the campus round. Between September and February that means a workshop series, a brand and pitch bootcamp, mentor matching, team matching for anyone arriving without one, checkpoints through the winter, and the Grand Finale itself in front of judges from the Windsor business community.

All of it is free. The top three teams take home $2,000, $1,000 and $500. The prizes and the winning team's travel are funded separately by the partners whose names they carry, so everything we raise for the program is spent on running it. Beyond the prizes, every team gets honest feedback from people who have built companies, and the winner earns a place at the National Championships and a route to the global final.
yearOne: The University of Windsor entered the Hult Prize for the first time in the 2025 to 2026 cycle, under founding Campus Director Godswisdom Ogbonna. Fourteen student startups registered. Six of them pitched at the Grand Finale in front of judges drawn from the Windsor business community.

Two teams, Mycovolt and 100% Fish, went on to the Canadian National Championships at McGill University in Montreal, where 100% Fish finished in the top eight in the country. At the close of the cycle the Hult Prize Foundation named the University of Windsor program the Best Program in North America, in its first year of operation.
For context, the Hult Prize runs at more than 2,200 universities and the field includes Harvard, Stanford, Columbia and McGill. The Windsor program ran on $8,000 and the support of ten partners.
yearPlan: Year one proved that Windsor students will show up, and that the best of them can compete nationally. Year two is about widening the field, holding it together through the winter, and putting a team in a position to win in April.

We are working toward twenty registered startups, at least ten teams on the Grand Finale stage, and a minimum of $10,000 raised to support them. Every one of those is a number we will report against afterwards.
yearBenefits: All of it is free, and none of it asks you to have anything ready in advance.

A workshop series on problem definition, business modelling, deck construction and pitch delivery. A brand and pitch bootcamp from late October to the end of November. A mentor matched to your team, someone who has actually built and run a business. Team matching if you arrive without one. Checkpoints through January, with a named person who follows up when a team goes quiet. A Grand Finale judged by people from the Windsor business community. And for the team that wins, eight weeks of preparation before the National Championships.
competeIntro: You do not need a company. You do not need a prototype, funding, or a business degree, and you certainly do not need a finished deck. What you need is an idea, two to four people, and the nerve to stand up for four minutes. We teach the rest between October and February, and none of it costs you anything.
Here is the part most people get wrong. Only one member of your team has to be enrolled at UWindsor. If you already build things with a friend at another university, bring them.
eligibility: Teams of two to four people.
Every member must be a student, undergraduate or graduate.
Everyone must be 18 or older at the time of registration.
At least one member must be enrolled at the University of Windsor. The others do not have to be.
Your venture must be for-profit and address at least one UN Sustainable Development Goal.
steps: 1. Sign up below. This is how we reach you about deadlines, workshops and team matching.
2. Register officially at hultprize.org/register. This is the only registration that counts toward the competition.
3. Sort your team. Two to four people. No team yet? See below. We match people and it works.
4. Join the group chat. Everything time-sensitive happens there.
5. Come to the workshops. They are free and you choose which ones to attend.
noTeam: Tell us your program and year, what you are good at, and whether you have an idea or want to join someone else's. We will introduce you to two or three people who fit. Mixed skills beat three people from the same program every single time.
faq: Does it cost anything?  No. Not to enter, and not to attend any part of it.
Is there a cash prize at the campus round?  Yes. The top three teams take home $2,000, $1,000 and $500. The winner also goes to the National Championships with travel covered.
Do I need to be in business school?  No. Last year's teams came from across the university, and mixed teams do better than single-program ones.
What if my idea changes?  Good. Most of them should, and the workshops are built around that.
How much time does this take?  Workshops run about an hour and you choose which to attend. The pitch itself is four minutes.
Can someone from another university be on my team?  Yes, as long as they are a student and at least one of you is enrolled at UWindsor.
partnersYear: Ten organisations funded this program in its first year. Fourteen student startups registered, six pitched at the Grand Finale, and two teams reached the National Championships at McGill, where 100% Fish finished top eight in Canada. The Hult Prize Foundation named Windsor the best program in North America.

This year we are aiming for twenty registered startups, at least ten teams pitching on February 5, and $10,000 to run the program. The prize money and the winning team's travel are sponsored separately and are not part of that figure.
partnersBenefits: Twenty startups means forty to eighty students who spent a term building a business alongside a full course load. Every partner gets the opt-in directory after the Grand Finale, with permission to contact them. If you hire students, this is the most useful thing on the page.

Three to four hours on February 5. You watch ten teams present, question them, and help decide which one represents Windsor at the National Championships. If you are hiring, it is a direct look at how people think under pressure.

Every partner gets a report within a month of the Grand Finale: the numbers, the photographs, the ventures by name, where the winning team placed, and what the money paid for. Written so you can use it in your own reporting.
partnersVentures: Fourteen ventures were built here last year. Two of them, Mycovolt and 100% Fish, went to the National Championships. Both are still operating today and both are still in Windsor, with their founders here.
If your organisation reports on economic development, talent retention or the local innovation ecosystem, that is something you can point at.
funding: Money raised for the program pays for the venue, the workshops, the bootcamp, the mentors, the materials and the Grand Finale itself. The cash prizes and the winning team's travel to Montreal are funded separately by the partners whose names they carry. How many teams we can support properly depends on what we raise.

Third Prize Partner, $500.  The third prize carries your name and is announced from the stage.
otherTiers: Gold Partner, $2,500.  A booth at the Grand Finale, placed for the twenty minutes between the last pitch and the results, when the room is full. A judging seat. Logo on the stage banner, website, Finals program and participant materials.

Supporter, $500.  Logo on the website and the Finals program, and thanks across our channels.
In kind, by agreement.  Legal hours, software or cloud credits, coworking space, accounting, design work, or travel support to Nationals. Recognised at the Gold level.
tierReport: Impact report within a month of the Grand Finale.
tierNote: All amounts in Canadian dollars. Any package can be adjusted. Partner logos are needed by January 5 for Grand Finale materials.
otherSupport: Judge on February 5. Mentor a team for two or three hours between December and late January, and we will handle the matching. Run a workshop in your own area. Offer space, a mention in a newsletter, or an introduction to someone who should know about this.
partnersContact: Tell us what you are trying to get out of this and we will build the package around it rather than pointing you at the next tier up.
contactIntro: Hult Prize UWindsor sits inside Fusion, a hub on campus for people building things. Our teams work there, argue about their business models there, and run into people building their own things. We run sessions and events out of it through the year.
It is ours, but it is not a closed door. If you are a UWindsor student with an idea, or half an idea, or you just want to see what this is, come and find us.
